t: Warning: Most Teachers Make This Classroom Management Mistake; Do You?
q: The mistake most teachers make is asking students why they misbehaved.
Jeffrey hems and haws and, like anyone caught behaving poorly, is not sure how to answer.
The reason Jeffery made the decision to stand on his chair is the same reason any of us behaves poorly: because, at the time, he wanted to.
Forcing an explanation from students causes resentment. To them it feels like humiliation. Yes, you have a right to handle misbehavior this way. But you’ll pay a price for it.
A better way to handle misbehavior is to hold students accountable with a consequence.
Four words, three seconds, one consequence and Mr. Shoemaker was done with the interaction.
If you notice a student lashing out against others, you may have to ask why in order to rule out retaliation against bullying—which can never be taken lightly.

t: How To Get Your Students To Listen To You
q: You give a single direction to a quiet and seemingly attentive classroom, and then watch as a third of your students either don’t know what to do, or they do it incorrectly.
This strategy so effective, in fact, that you can use it with a group of students you’ve just met, and they’ll follow your directions like a champion drill team.
The way the strategy works is that you get your students listening to simple and physical directions first before giving more important directions.
If at this point all of your students are following along, slide in your important directions.
It also has staying power. Although it takes less than a minute, you won’t have to use it all the time. Just use it a couple of times a week or whenever you need it.
The “simple first” strategy is effective because it trains students to listen for the sound of your voice and to follow directions precisely and the first time they’re given.

t: How To Turn Around Difficult Students (Part 3) https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2010/03/13/difficult-students-turning-them-around-part-3/
q: This third and final part of this series is about communicating with difficult students in a way that will compel them to behave the way you want them to.

In dealing with difficult students, teachers become frustrated and react by scolding, yelling, and threatening. True, these methods may suppress behavior in the short term, but they do nothing to improve behavior over time.

When difficult students do something correctly, teachers tend to praise too much or too demonstratively. They hug, cheer, high-five, celebrate, and give rewards and prizes—often for expected behavior.
Your goal with difficult students should be to build influence with them. When a student likes and trusts you, they’ll want to behave in a way that pleases you.
A good rule of thumb is to not spend any more time on them than the rest of your students.
It’s a myth that having fun somehow causes students to misbehave. The opposite is true.
If you build influence with difficult students, and you’re committed to holding them accountable when they misbehave, you can completely and unalterably turn them around.

t: How To Turn Around Difficult Students (Part 2)
q: Most so-called difficult students need nothing more than a teacher with a solid classroom management plan and a thorough understanding of how to implement and enforce it.

Teachers who make decisions based on feeling sorry for students and their sometimes-awful circumstances can cause behavior to worsen. The most compassionate thing you can do for a difficult student is to hold him or her accountable.
When your students enter your classroom, pull the student in question aside and inform her that she is no longer a member of your classroom.
For the first week, leave Jennifer alone. No pep talks. No lectures. No profound words. Don’t tell her what to think or how to feel.
We all want to feel like we are part of something. No student is immune from this desire. This is why the more camaraderie, rapport, and fun you can create in your classroom the better.
She has to prove to you she’s ready. Does she talk about her mistakes? Does she apologize? Does she discuss how she is going to handle herself in the future?
After your conversation, move her desk back and let her rejoin her classmates as a member in good standing.
